 1         1.      Jurisdiction & Service

 2          This Court has subject matter jurisdiction pursuant to the Class Action Fairness Act, 28

 3   U.S.C. § 1332(d). The aggregated claims of the individual class members exceed the sum or

 4   value of $5,000,000.00, exclusive of interest and costs; there are more than 100 putative class

 5   members; and at least one putative class member is from a state different from Defendant.

 6   Defendant’s motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction (ECF No. 17) and motion to

 7   transfer venue (ECF No. 20) are both pending.

 8         2.      Facts

 9          Plaintiffs’ Position:

10          This class action is filed in response to Defendant American Airlines, Inc.’s

11   (“Defendant”) wrongful termination of Plaintiffs’ and the putative class members’ AAdvantage

12   program accounts. Plaintiffs allege Defendant materially breached its contracts with class

13   members, resulting in the wrongful termination of airline reward miles and, thus, resulting in

14   the loss of significant monetary value. Plaintiffs lawfully accrued their AAdvantage award

15   miles through (1) purchases of consumer goods and services, (2) purchases of Defendant’s

16   flights, and (3) credit card enrollment bonuses. Plaintiffs are all California residents seeking to

17   recover damages for ongoing injuries sustained in California.

18          Defendant’s Position:

19          Defendant American Airlines, Inc. launched the first loyalty program of any major

20   carrier, pioneering the concept of the “frequent-flyer” program, called AAdvantage. The

21   AAdvantage program is governed by Terms & Conditions that are publicly available on

22   American’s website.      Plaintiffs are former AAdvantage members whose accounts were

23   terminated for fraud, misrepresentation, and/or abuse of the AAdvantage program. American

24   offered certain existing AAdvantage members the opportunity to receive “bonus” miles in their

25   accounts by using one-time codes from direct mailers for promotional credit cards. (See First

26   Amended Complaint, ECF No. 14, ¶ 21.) Plaintiffs opened multiple American-branded credit

27   cards using mailers that were not sent to them or meant for them. Rather, Plaintiffs admit that

28   they used promotional offers that were sent to friends and family members in opening these

                  JOINT CASE MANAGEMENT STATEMENT | CASE NO.: 5:24-CV-00530-PCP
                                            -2-
           Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 38 Filed 04/18/24 Page 3 of 11




 1    accounts. (Id. ¶¶ 57, 83, 101, 128.) American terminated their accounts due to “violations of

 2    the General AAdvantage Program Conditions … related to the accrual of ineligible miles and

 3    benefits; through fraud, misrepresentation and/or abuse of the AAdvantage Program.” (Id. ¶¶

 4    74, 92, 118, 143.) At the time their accounts were terminated, Plaintiffs Ari and Shanna

 5    Nachison resided in California, (id. ¶¶ 54, 80) and Plaintiffs Derrick Gallagher and Abigail

 6    Gallagher resided in Missouri (id. ¶¶ 98, 125.)

 7          3.      Legal Issues

 8          Plaintiffs’ Position

 9          Plaintiffs originally brought claims for breach of contract and unjust enrichment. Plaintiffs

10   have since conceded that the unjust enrichment claim—and only that claim—is preempted. Thus,

11   Plaintiffs’ remaining claim is for breach of contract. The legal and factual issues include, but are

12   not limited to, the following:

13          a.      Whether Class Members performed pursuant to Defendant’s offer when they

14   opened a Citi-AAdvantage credit card or Barclays-AAdvantage credit card accounts and fulfilled

15   the enrollment bonus requirements;

16          b.      Whether a contract was formed at the time when a Class Member opened a

17   AAdvantage account;

18          c.      Whether a contract was formed at the time when a Class Member opened a Citi-

19   AAdvantage credit card or Barclays-AAdvantage credit card account;

20          d.      Whether Defendant wrongfully terminated Class Members’ AAdvantage

21   accounts;

22          e.      Whether Defendant wrongfully forced Class Members to forfeit earned miles,

23   including miles that had been accrued before their application for, opening of, or use of a Citi-

24   AAdvantage credit card or Barclays-AAdvantage credit card; and

25           f.      Whether Defendant breached the contract when it wrongfully terminated

26   AAdvantage accounts and forced the forfeiture of earned miles.

27           Defendant’s Position

28           a.      What provision of the Terms & Conditions did American allegedly breach?

                   JOINT CASE MANAGEMENT STATEMENT | CASE NO.: 5:24-CV-00530-PCP
                                             -3-
           Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 38 Filed 04/18/24 Page 4 of 11




 1           b.      Was American justified in terminating Plaintiffs’ AAdvantage accounts because

 2   they engaged in fraud, misrepresentation, and abuse?

 3           c.      Whether Plaintiffs’ or putative absent class members’ claims are barred by

 4   applicable statutes of limitation?

 5           d.      Whether Plaintiffs’ or putative absent class members’ claims are otherwise

 6   barred by their inequitable conduct?

 7           e.      If Plaintiffs could somehow establish liability, is any remedy available other

 8   than reinstatement of their AAdvantage memberships?

 9          4.      Motions

10            Defendant has two fully briefed and pending motions: (1) a Motion to Dismiss for lack

11    of personal jurisdiction (ECF No. 17); and (2) a Motion to Transfer Venue (ECF No. 20). The

12    motions are noticed for hearing on May 2, 2024. Plaintiffs anticipate filing a motion for class

13    certification. Defendant will oppose any motion for class certification and anticipates filing a

14    motion for summary judgment.

15          5.      Amendment of Pleadings

16            Plaintiffs reserve the right to seek leave of court to amend their Complaint in response

17    to any Court order regarding Defendant’s currently pending motions. In light of its pending

18    motion to dismiss (ECF No. 17), Defendant has not yet filed an Answer.

19          6.      Evidence Preservation

20            The parties have reviewed the Northern District ESI guidelines, ESI checklist, and have

21    met and conferred regarding steps to preserve ESI evidence. The parties also agreed to discuss

22    in detail such methods with respect to specific issues arising in connection with production of

23    documents. Defendant has advised Plaintiffs that relevant personnel who may have

24    discoverable materials in their possession have been advised to retain all available potentially

25    relevant information on issues related to claims raised in this litigation. Defendant has also

26    implemented adequate safeguards to ensure that potentially relevant ESI, which was available

27    at the time this lawsuit was filed, is preserved.

28

 1          7.      Disclosures

 2          Defendant filed its Corporate Disclosure Statement on March 4, 2024 (ECF No. 18). The

 3   parties agree that they will mutually exchange Rule 26 initial disclosures within 14 days after the

 4   May 2, 2024 Case Management Conference.

 5          8.      Discovery

 6          Plaintiffs’ Position

 7          There has been no formal or informal discovery exchange to date. The parties do not

 8   anticipate proposing any significant limitations or modifications of the discovery rules. Plaintiffs

 9   propose the schedule set forth below. Plaintiffs intend to serve document requests, admissions

10   requests, and interrogatories, and to conduct depositions of Defendant and non-party witnesses

11   who may have knowledge regarding all issues regarding, or related to, the allegations set forth in

12   Plaintiffs’ Complaint. Plaintiffs further anticipate seeking discovery regarding Defendant’s

13   affirmative defenses and experts. Because Defendant has not moved to dismiss the breach of

14   contract claims brought by Plaintiffs Ari and Shana Nachison, Plaintiffs maintain that discovery

15   should be permitted to commence immediately. Any burden potentially imposed on Defendant

16   through the immediate commencement of discovery is vitiated by the fact that Defendant has not

17   moved to dismiss some of Plaintiffs’ claims. Thus, there is no reason for delaying discovery.

18          Defendant’s Position

19          Defendant believes that engaging in discovery while its motion to dismiss (ECF No. 17)

20   and motion to transfer venue (ECF No. 20) are pending could impose unnecessary burdens and

21   expense on the parties and the Court in the event one of those motions is granted part.

22   Accordingly, Defendant proposes that, with the exception of exchanging initial disclosures, fact

23   discovery shall not commence until the date on which the Court issues its final decision on its

24   motion to dismiss and motion to transfer. In Paragraph 16, Defendant has proposed a schedule

25   of deadlines to complete fact and expert discovery.

26          9.      Class Actions

27          All attorneys of record have reviewed the Northern District’s Procedural Guidance for

28   Class Action Settlements. In accordance with the schedule proposed below, Plaintiffs anticipate

 1   filing a class certification motion within approximately eighteen (18) months of the court’s ruling

 2   on the motion to dismiss. Defendant intends to oppose any motion for class certification.

 3          10.       Related Cases

 4          Neither party is presently aware of any related cases.

 5          11.       Relief

 6          Plaintiffs’ Position

 7          The prayer to the First Amended Complaint seeks the following relief on behalf of

 8   Plaintiffs and members of the proposed Class:

 9          a.        Determine that the claims alleged herein may be maintained as a class action under

10   Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23, and issuance of an order certifying one or more classes as

11   defined above;

12          b.        Appoint Plaintiffs as the representatives of the Class and their counsel as Class

13   Counsel;

14          c.        Award actual, general, special, incidental, statutory, punitive, and consequential

15   damages and restitution to which Plaintiffs and the Class Members are entitled;

16          d.        Award pre-judgment and post-judgment interest on such monetary relief;

17          e.        Award reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs; and

18          f.        Grant such further relief that this Court deems appropriate.

19          Defendant’s Position

20          Defendant denies that Plaintiffs are entitled to their requested relief. Any requested relief,

21   moreover, is limited by the terms and conditions of the AAdvantage Program.

22          Defendant reserves its rights to seek recovery of its attorney’s fees and costs as provided

23   by applicable law.

24          12.       Settlement and ADR

25          The parties met and conferred regarding ADR and submitted their ADR Certifications,

26   pursuant to Civil L.R. 16-8(b) and ADR L.R. 3-5 (b). (ECF Nos. 30-35.) The Parties agree that

27   ADR is premature at this time. However, at the appropriate time, if the parties are amenable to

 2   ADR provider would be the parties’ preferred ADR option.

 4           The parties agree that this case is not suitable for assignment to binding arbitration, special

 1   I.       INTRODUCTION
 2            Plaintiffs seek to litigate this case in the Northern District of California on behalf of a
 3   putative nationwide class, alleging breach of a contract that was drafted and administered in
 4   Texas. Defendant American Airlines, Inc. (“American”) moved to transfer this action, in part,
 5   because six of the eight named Plaintiffs’ claims had no nexus to this jurisdiction and thus would
 6   otherwise need to be dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction. To avoid transfer, four of those
 7   plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their claims.
 8            Now, the remaining Plaintiffs assert that American’s arguments for transfer lack merit
 9   because there is no longer a jurisdictional defect to be remedied. Plaintiffs’ gambit to avoid
10   transfer fails. To start, they did not moot the jurisdictional issues that strongly support transfer.
11   Two of the remaining named Plaintiffs, the Gallaghers, bring claims based solely on events that
12   occurred outside of the Northern District of California. Their claims can be heard in Texas, but
13   they cannot be heard here. The same is true of absent class members whose claims do not relate
14   to American’s contacts with California, including all the former named plaintiffs who voluntarily
15   dismissed their claims. See Opp. 5-6 n.3 (acknowledging potential issues with nationwide class
16   in California).
17            Moreover, regardless of the jurisdictional issues, the majority of the factors under Jones v.
18   GNC Franchising, Inc., 211 F.3d 495 (9th Cir. 2000), favor transfer to the Northern District of
19   Texas. Plaintiffs’ single claim involves a contract that was drafted (and allegedly breached) at
20   American’s corporate headquarters in Texas and is governed by Texas law. Texas also serves as
21   a more convenient forum for the potential witnesses in this case—many of whom are located in
22   Texas and subject to the compulsory process there.
23            Accordingly, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), American respectfully requests that the
24   Court transfer venue to the Northern District of Texas, Fort Worth Division.
25   II.      ARGUMENT
26            Plaintiffs do not appear to dispute that this action could have been brought in the Northern
27   District of Texas. Nor could they. See Mot. 3. Plaintiffs instead contend that American has

 3           B.      The Jones Factors Strongly Favor Transfer.

 4           Even if there were no jurisdictional issues, this case should be transferred because the
 5   majority of the Jones factors support transfer. Plaintiffs’ main point in opposition—repeated
 6   throughout their brief—seems to be the inconvenience and expense of litigating a case in Texas
 7   while residing and working in California. Plaintiffs’ concerns are significantly exaggerated and
 8   overlook the realities of litigation.
 9           Plaintiffs will only be required to travel to Texas if this case proceeds to trial, which will
10   likely be short. They can be deposed in California. And all other aspects of this case that require
11   travel to Texas can be handled by their lawyers. While their lawyers (two of whom are in
12   Knoxville, and all of whom are from outside this District) might be slightly inconvenienced by
13   traveling to Texas, “[j]udges in this District have repeatedly stated that the location of plaintiff’s
14   counsel is not an appropriate factor for the Court to consider when deciding a motion to transfer.”
15   See Wilson v. Walgreen Co., 2011 WL 4345079, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 14, 2011). “Even to the
16   extent the Court considers the convenience of counsel indirectly—i.e., because of the financial
17   burdens on the litigants and their interest in using their established counsel—that does not tip the
18   scales in Plaintiffs’ favor. There is no evidence that Plaintiffs themselves (as opposed to their
19   counsel) will directly incur costs.” Id. (internal citations omitted). In short, Plaintiffs’ core
20   position is that transfer is unwarranted because they would be inconvenienced by traveling to a
21   hypothetical future trial in Texas about a contract they entered into with a Texas company that
22   was drafted and administered in the company’s headquarters in Texas. That is not a persuasive
23   argument, and the Jones factors, considered as a whole, strongly support transfer.
24                   1.      Location where the relevant agreements were negotiated and executed

25           Plaintiffs contend that this factor is “neutral” because half the contracts were negotiated
26   and breached in this District and half were not. Opp. 3. But this factor is not neutral. While the
27   location of negotiation and breach might be a wash, “the location of the drafting may [also] be a

 9   transferee district.” Opp. 3. But this overstates American’s reliance on that case. Mot. 3-4.
10   Martindale-Hubbell stands for the more modest proposition that the location of drafting is a
11   relevant consideration where the parties were not in the same physical location, a point not even
12   Plaintiffs dispute. And that consideration favors transfer.
13                   2.     The state that is most familiar with the governing law

14           Plaintiffs argue that this Court is capable of applying Texas contract law. American
15   agrees. But the second Jones factor does not ask whether the transferor court can apply the
16   governing law, but instead, which state “is most familiar with the governing law.” Jones 211
17   F.3d at 498 (emphasis added); Synopsys, Inc. v. Mentor Graphics Corp., 2013 WL 1365946, at *5
18   (N.D. Cal. Apr. 3, 2013) (finding that the second Jones factor weighed in favor of transfer where
19   “the Oregon court has considerably more familiarity with Oregon contract law, which governs the
20   interpretation of the Settlement Agreement”). Plaintiffs do not meaningfully address American’s
21   argument that Texas courts are most familiar with Texas contract law. This factor also weighs in
22   favor of transfer.
23                  3.      Plaintiffs’ choice of forum

24          This Court should give Plaintiffs’ choice of forum less weight because they seek to
25   represent a nationwide class. Lou v. Belzberg, 834 F.2d 730, 739 (9th Cir. 1987); Hoefert v. Am.
26   Airlines, Inc., 2018 WL 2740276, at *2 (D. Ariz. June 7, 2018). Plaintiffs do not dispute that
27   “deference can be diminished in the context of a class action.” Opp. 5. Their only dispute is

16   contacts with this jurisdiction, American’s contacts also inform the analysis. Plaintiffs contend

22   not all California residents, supports transfer. See Roberts v. CR England, Inc., 827 F. Supp. 2d
23   1078, 1087 (N.D. Cal. 2011) (“On balance, the fourth factor—the parties’ respective contacts
24   with the forum—also favors Utah. Defendants have greater contacts with Utah, where they are
25   headquartered. Although Roberts and McKay live in California, they seek to represent a
26   nationwide class of drivers, many of whom may not have had contact with this district, but likely
27   have had contact with Utah.”).

 3                   6.      Differences in the costs of litigation in the two forums

 4           According to Plaintiffs, because American is a “large corporation and the largest airline in
 5   the United States,” it can absorb litigation costs better than Plaintiffs. Id. at 8-9. Plaintiffs
 6   misconstrue the sixth Jones factor, which considers “the differences in the costs of litigation in
 7   the two forums.” Jones, 211 F.3d at 498-99. If the only concern were the parties’ relative

 9   District of Texas offers the most cost-effective forum because the majority of the witnesses will
10   likely be its former and current employees, most of whom are located there. See Mot. 6; Park v.
11   Dole Fresh Vegetables, Inc., 964 F. Supp. 2d 1088, 1095 (N.D. Cal. 2013) (“Generally, litigation

18   named plaintiffs “and certain drivers and witnesses live in California” but “[t]he remaining
19   drivers live in locations throughout the United States. Utah is more centrally located than this
20   district.”).

 1   I.     INTRODUCTION

 2           This class action is filed in response to Defendant American Airlines, Inc.’s

 3   (“Defendant”) wrongful termination of Plaintiffs’ and the putative class members’ AAdvantage

 4   program accounts. Plaintiffs allege Defendant materially breached its contracts with class

 5   members, resulting in the wrongful termination of airline reward miles and, thus, resulting in the

 6   loss of significant monetary value. Plaintiffs lawfully accrued their AAdvantage award miles

 7   through (1) purchases of consumer goods and services, (2) purchases of Defendant’s flights, and

 8   (3) credit card enrollment bonuses. Plaintiffs are all California residents seeking to recover

 9   damages for ongoing injuries sustained in California.

10          Defendant moved to dismiss the claims of six of the named Plaintiffs—Derrick Gallagher,

11   Abigail Gallagher, Eric Link, Miranda Link, Elliott Weiner, and Rachel Feit—for lack of personal

12   jurisdiction.1 See Defendant’s Motion to Dismiss (“Defendant’s Motion”), ECF No. 17, at 5-7.

13   Id. at 7-11. In an effort to narrow the issues in dispute, Plaintiffs Eric Link, Miranda Link, Elliott

14   Weiner, and Rachel Feit have moved to voluntarily dismiss their claims. ECF Nos. 23-26.

15          Defendant moves to dismiss the claims of the Derrick Gallagher’s and Plaintiff Abigail

16   Gallagher’s (the “Gallagher Plaintiffs”) because “[t]hey are suing a non-California defendant on

17   contracts that were entered into and allegedly breached outside California.” Defendant’s Motion

18   at 1.2 Thus, Defendant’s argument in support of dismissal of the Gallagher Plaintiffs remain

19   undisturbed.

20
     1 Defendant also moved to dismiss Plaintiffs’ unjust enrichment claim, arguing that it is
21   preempted. After a thorough analysis of relevant case law in the context of the allegations here,
22   Plaintiffs acknowledge that the Airline Deregulation Act (“ADA”) preempts unjust enrichment
     claims and concede this issue. However, as Defendant acknowledges, “the ADA does not
23   preempt [the] breach of contract claims” brought by Plaintiffs in this Action. Defendant’s Motion
     at 8-9 (emphasis in original).
24
     2 Defendant has not moved to dismiss Plaintiff Ari Nachison’s and Plaintiff Shanna Nachison’s
25
     (the “Nachison Plaintiffs”) claims for lack of personal jurisdiction. Thus, even if the Court were
26   to determine that it lacks personal jurisdiction as to the remaining Plaintiffs—and Plaintiffs
     contend that this Court can properly exercise personal jurisdiction over the Gallagher Plaintiffs,
27   see infra Section III.A.—the Nachison Plaintiffs’ claims and those of the putative class members
     would remain.

                           IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT’S MOTION TO DISMISS

 1          Defendant’s contention for dismissal relies exclusively on Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v.

 2   Superior Court to argue that this Court cannot exercise personal jurisdiction over these specific

 3   Plaintiffs’ claims because their claims do not arise out of or relate to Defendant’s activities in

 4   California. Id. at 5 (citing Bristol-Myers, 582 U.S. 255, 262 (2017)). As discussed below, Ninth

 5   Circuit case law accords with the overwhelming weight of authority since Bristol-Myers holding

 6   that its limitations do not apply to class actions brought in federal court. This Court may exercise

 7   jurisdiction over absent class members, including the named California Plaintiffs and potentially

 8   out-of-state class members as well. See, e.g., Fitzhenry-Russell v. Dr. Pepper Snapple Grp., Inc.,

 9   2017 WL 4224723 (N.D. Cal. Sep. 22, 2017) (rejecting the argument that Bristol-Myers precludes

10   a court from exercising personal jurisdiction over the claims of absent class members who are

11   out-of-state); In re Chinese-Manufactured Drywall Prods. Liability Litig., 2017 WL 5971622, at

12   *12-13 (E.D. La. Nov. 30, 2017) (same); cf. Swamy v. Title Source, Inc., Case No. 17-01175

13   WHA, 2017 WL 5196780 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 10, 2017) (rejecting the argument that Bristol-Myers

14   precludes a court from exercising personal jurisdiction over the claims of out-of-state opt-in

15   plaintiffs in a collective action). Here, Plaintiffs Ari Nachison, Shanna Nachison, Derrick

16   Gallagher, and Abigail Gallagher are all California residents and putative class representatives

17   bringing actions in federal court seeking redress for continuing harm occurring in California (and

18   nationwide). Defendant does not—and cannot—present any precedential support for dismissing

19   the claims of these California residents on jurisdictional grounds.

20          Notably, Defendant does not argue that this court lacks personal jurisdiction over the

21   Nachison Plaintiffs, presumably in large part because they are California residents. Cf.

22   Defendant’s Motion at 5-7. Similarly, the Gallagher Plaintiffs are residents of California whose

23   claims are properly brought in this Court. In addition to establishing personal jurisdiction over

24   Defendant independently, the Gallagher Plaintiffs can rely on the doctrine of “pendent personal

25   jurisdiction,” which establishes that “a court may assert pendent personal jurisdiction over a

26   defendant with respect to a claim for which there is no independent basis of personal jurisdiction

27   so long as it arises out of a common nucleus of operative facts with a claim in the same suit over

28                       PLAINTIFFS’ MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

                                           5:24-CV-00530-PCP

 1   which the court does have personal jurisdiction.” Sloan v. General Motors LLC, 287 F. Supp. 3d

 2   840, 860 (N.D. Cal. 2018) ( “Sloan I”) (quoting Action Embroidery Corp. v. Atl. Embroidery,

 3   Inc., 368 F.3d 1174, 1180 (9th Cir. 2004)). Defendant has failed to provide any relevant, much

 4   less controlling, precedent to support dismissing the claims of the Nachison Plaintiffs or Gallagher

 5   Plaintiffs—all California residents—on jurisdictional grounds. Therefore, Defendant’s motion to

 6   dismiss should be denied.

 7   II.     STATEMENT OF RELEVANT FACTS

 8           Defendant launched its frequent flyer program, AAdvantage, in 1981. First Amended

 9   Complaint (“FAC”), ECF No. 14, ¶ 16. Members of the program can earn award miles and then

10   use those miles to purchase program benefits such as flights, flight upgrades, car rentals, hotels,

11   and other products. Id. ¶ 17. One of the most significant ways an AAdvantage member can earn

12   miles is through obtaining a Defendant’s branded credit card. Id. ¶ 21. Often, these branded credit

13   cards offer enrollment bonuses for AAdvantage members, based on qualifying purchases with the

14   credit card within a specified period. Id. ¶ 25-26. Defendant encourages AAdvantage members to

15   open and use these credit cards by sending promotional enrollment bonus offers to members via

16   mail and email. Id. ¶ 32, 36. Importantly, some of these promotional offers contained “Offer

17   Availability” restrictions which limited the amount of enrollment bonuses a customer could

18   receive during a 48-month period, while others did not contain any such restriction. Id. ¶¶ 33-35.

19           Plaintiffs Ari Nachison, Shanna Nachison, Derrick Gallagher, and Abigail Gallagher each

20   maintained an individual AAdvantage account. Id. ¶¶ 55, 81, 99, 126. As AAdvantage members,

21   they each received promotional materials inviting them to open Defendant’s branded credit cards.

22   Id. ¶¶ 57, 83, 101, 128. Based on these offers, they opened branded credit cards and made

23   qualifying purchases within the required time period to earn enrollment bonuses. Id. ¶¶ 58-70,

24   84-90, 102-114, 129-141. Notably, none of the promotional offers used by the Plaintiffs contained

25   offer availability or transferability restrictions. Id. ¶¶ 57, 83, 101, 128. Despite Plaintiffs lawfully

26   opening their Defendant’s branded credit cards and spending money to fulfill the enrollment

27   bonus requirements, Defendant sent emails notifying each of the Plaintiffs that their AAdvantage

 1   accounts had been terminated and all award miles (and tickets purchased with award miles) were

 2   forfeited. Id. ¶¶ 74, 92, 118, 143. As a result of Defendant’s wrongful and unilateral termination

 3   of Plaintiffs’ AAdvantage accounts, Plaintiffs suffered actual damages in the form of lost miles

 4   and cancelled flights, incurring economic harm.

 5   III.    ARGUMENT

 6           A.     This Court May Exercise Specific Personal Jurisdiction Over Defendant for
                    Claims by California Residents.
 7
             “Federal courts ordinarily follow state law in determining the bounds of their jurisdiction
 8
     over persons.” Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117, 125 (2014). “Because California’s long-
 9
     arm statute allows the exercise of personal jurisdiction to the full extent permissible under the
10
     U.S. Constitution, [the Court’s] inquiry centers on whether exercising jurisdiction comports with
11
     due process.” Glob. Commodities Trading Grp., Inc. v. Beneficio de Arroz Choloma, S.A., 972
12
     F.3d 1101, 1106 (9th Cir. 2020) (internal quotation marks omitted). “Federal due process permits
13
     a court to exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident defendant if that defendant has ‘at least
14
     ‘minimum contacts’ with the relevant forum such that the exercise of jurisdiction ‘does not offend
15
     traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.’” Id. (quoting Schwarzenegger v. Fred
16
     Martin Motor Co., 374 F.3d 797, 801 (9th Cir. 2004)). A court’s basis for personal jurisdiction
17
     may either be “general,” when a defendant is essentially at home in the forum, or “specific,” for
18
     “issues deriving from, or connected with, the very controversy that establishes jurisdiction.” Id.
19
     at 1106-07. Here, the facts support the application of specific personal jurisdiction over
20
     Defendant.
21
             “The inquiry whether a forum State may assert specific jurisdiction over a nonresident
22
     defendant focuses on the relationship among the defendant, the forum, and the litigation.” Herbal
23
     Brands, Inc. v. Photoplaza, Inc., 72 F.4th 1085, 1090 (9th Cir. 2023). In analyzing specific
24
     personal jurisdiction, the Ninth Circuit has established a three-part test:
25
             (1) The non-resident defendant must purposefully direct his activities or
26           consummate some transaction with the forum or resident thereof; or perform some
             act by which he purposefully avails himself of the privilege of conducting activities
27           in the forum, thereby invoking the benefits and protections of its laws; (2) the claim
             must be one which arises out of or relates to the defendant’s forum-related
28                       PLAINTIFFS’ MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
                           IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT’S MOTION TO DISMISS
                                           5:24-CV-00530-PCP
                                                       4
           Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 27 Filed 04/01/24 Page 9 of 22



            activities; and (3) the exercise of jurisdiction must comport with fair play and
 1          substantial justice, i.e. it must be reasonable.

 2
     Id. Once the plaintiff has established the first two prongs, “the burden then shifts to the defendant
 3
     to present a compelling case that the exercise of jurisdiction would not be reasonable.” Id.
 4
     (internal quotation marks omitted).
 5
                    1.      Defendant purposefully availed itself of the privilege of conducting
 6                          business in California.
 7          Under the first prong this specific personal jurisdiction test, “both purposeful availment
 8   and purposeful direction ask whether defendants have voluntarily derived some benefit from their
 9   interstate activities such that they ‘will not be hauled into a jurisdiction solely as a result of
10   ‘random,’ ‘fortuitous,’ or ‘attenuated’ contacts.’” Global Commodities, 972 F.3d at 1107 (quoting
11   Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462, 474-75 (1985)). Purposeful availment “exists
12   when a defendant’s dealings with a state establishes a ‘quid pro quo’—where the defendant
13   ‘purposefully avails itself of the privilege of conducting activities within the forum State, thus
14   invoking the benefits and protections of its laws,’ and in return ‘submit[s] to the burdens of
15   litigation’ in the State.” Davis v. Cranfield Aerospace Sols., Ltd., 71 F.4th 1154, 1163 (9th Cir.
16   2023), cert. denied, No. 23-775, 2024 WL 674875 (___ S. Ct. ___, Feb. 20, 2024) (quoting
17   Schwarzenegger v. Fred Martin Motor Co., 374 F.3d 797, 802 (9th Cir. 2004)).
18          Here, there is no question that Defendant has purposefully availed itself of the privilege
19   of conducting business in California such that the Court may exercise specific personal
20   jurisdiction. Not only does Defendant conduct substantial business in California and in this
21   District by operating flights into and out of the San Francisco International Airport, it “is
22   registered to do business in California.” FAC ¶ 12. Through this registration, Defendant has
23   purposefully availed itself of the privileges to conduct business in California. Moreover, through
24   its ongoing business—including through allowing California residents to enroll in AAdvantage
25   accounts, to fly on Defendant’s flights into and out of California, to accrue AAdvantage bonus
26   miles through their purchases, and to open Defendant’s branded credit cards using their California
27   addresses (including based on promotional materials sent by Defendant to California residents)—
28                       PLAINTIFFS’ MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
                           IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT’S MOTION TO DISMISS
                                           5:24-CV-00530-PCP
                                                       5
          Case 5:24-cv-00530-PCP Document 27 Filed 04/01/24 Page 10 of 22




 1   Defendant has purposefully directed its business to the state, leaving it undeniably open to being

 2   subject to this litigation. More to the point—and perhaps dispositively—Defendant has not argued

 3   that the Nachison Plaintiffs’ claims should be dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction. See

 4   generally Defendant’s Motion. As to the Nachison Plaintiffs, who are California residents,

 5   Defendant does not appear to argue that it is beyond the reach of this Court’s personal

 6   jurisdiction—and they may not raise this argument now. If Defendant concedes that it is subject

 7   to this Court’s jurisdiction in responding to the claims of certain California resident Plaintiffs,

 8   then it is likewise subject to the specific personal jurisdiction arising from claims of other

 9   California resident Plaintiffs, like the Gallagher Plaintiffs.

10                   2.      The Gallagher Plaintiffs’ claims relate to Defendant’s California-
                             related activities.
11
             The Gallagher Plaintiffs have also satisfied the second prong of the specific personal
12
     jurisdiction inquiry by demonstrating that their claims relate to Defendant’s California-related
13
     activities.3 In Ford Motor, the Supreme Court foreclosed the view that specific personal
14
     jurisdiction requires a strict causal relationship between a defendant’s forum-related activities and
15
     the litigation. Ayla, LLC v. Alya Skin Pty. Ltd., 11 F.4th 972, 983 n.5 (9th Cir. 2021) (citing Ford
16
     Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct., 592 U.S. 351 (2021)). Additionally, the Supreme
17
     Court has “never framed the specific jurisdiction inquiry as always requiring proof of causation—
18
     i.e., proof that the plaintiff’s claim came about because of the defendant’s in-state conduct.” Ford
19
     Motor Co., 592 U.S. at 362.
20
             In support of its motion to dismiss the Gallagher Plaintiffs’ claims, Defendant relies
21
     entirely on Bristol-Myers. Defendant’s Motion 6. But since that case was first decided, courts,
22
     including the Supreme Court, have drawn “important distinctions” with Bristol-Myers. Daimler
23
     Trucks North America LLC v. Sup. Ct. of Los Angeles, No. B316199, 296 Cal. Rptr. 3d 564, 574
24
     (Cal. Ct. App. July 7, 2022) (citing Ford Motor Co., 592 U.S. at 369-70). Courts must consider
25
26
     3 As noted, Defendant does not challenge personal jurisdiction as to the Nachison Plaintiffs. See
27   generally Defendant’s Motion at 5-7.
28                        PLAINTIFFS’ MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
                            IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT’S MOTION TO DISMISS

                                                        6

 1   other factors, such as the “plaintiff’s residence,” which “can be relevant in assessing the link

 2   between the defendant’s forum contacts and the plaintiff’s suit.” Id. (quoting Ford Motor Co.,

 3   592 U.S. at 371)). Because the Gallagher Plaintiffs currently reside in California, this

 4   consideration is relevant and weighs in favor of maintaining their claims in California before this

 5   Court.

 6            Defendant argues that there is no link between the Gallaghers’ claims and California

 7   because they “do not allege that Defendant instituted the credit-card reward program from

 8   California or terminated AAdvantage memberships in California.” Defendant’s Motion 6. But

 9   this argument, again, relies on Bristol-Myers while ignoring intervening precedent. Rather than

10   Bristol-Myers, this case is more akin to Ford Motor Company—a case that considered Bristol-

11   Myers and reached a different jurisdictional conclusion. In Ford Motor Company, the plaintiffs

12   brought product liability claims against Ford in Minnesota and Montana. 592 U.S. at 354-55.4

13   The plaintiffs, who were residents of Minnesota and Montana and were injured in car accidents

14   in those states, brought suit in state court in their respective home states. Id. at 355. Ford, however,

15   “contend[ed] that jurisdiction [was] improper because the particular car involved in the crash was

16   not first sold in the forum State, nor was it designed or manufactured there.” Id. The Supreme

17   Court agreed with the lower courts, rejecting such an argument. Id. at 357. The Court held that

18   Ford had indisputably purposefully availed itself in both Minnesota and Montana by selling its

19   vehicles in each state, advertising its vehicles in each state, repairing its vehicles in each state,

20   and “encouraging” consumers in each state to purchase Ford vehicles. Id. at 357, 361. In short,
